title: Implement discoverable host APIs, app backend operations and script tools
body:
Installed apps cannot reliably discover host APIs, register their own backend operations, or execute their own declared tools. This implements ADR 0012: versioned API discovery and compatibility checks; signed, app-owned backend registration and named requests; device consent; and tool dispatch into the app's existing full UI VM.

Backend GET operations can run for the owning account in background turns. Writes require native review of the exact request and a physical approval. Registration changes, account changes and withdrawal revoke stale access. Tokens stay in the host vault. Device widgets respect per-app consent independently of Android/macOS package permission, and background agents cannot open approval sheets.

Script tools retain the signed app identity, account, storage jail and bounded VM. Results are schema checked and bounded; close/account changes invalidate replies. Pending script calls and their results recheck signed admission for both owner and app caller so withdrawn or modified bundles cannot receive stale data. Closed apps return `app_not_running`. The runtime bridge bounds request serialization/queues and preserves nonprompting policy through host callbacks, detached timers, tasks, paused continuations, widget callbacks and HTTP/WebSocket callbacks, including native device helpers. Fresh foreground entries retain their own authority. Linux/Windows WebReader now reports unavailable explicitly.

The build pins public App Hub and renderer commits and published crates.io contract 1.6.0; no private dependency overrides are needed. Bilingual service docs, architecture notes and ADR 0012 describe the behavior and limits.

Validation on macOS:
- Public dependency/setup verification passed. Local-CI workflow mapping and all 117 tooling tests passed; desktop packaging tests: 10 passed.
- Desktop and Home packaging checks passed with `mobile-apps`.
- Full shell suite: 1,005 passed (including late owner/caller admission vetoes); the earlier focused app-tool suite had 22 passed.
- CI evidence directories are now unique and outside Cargo’s restored cache. The exact workflow command passed twice using the same runner temporary directory (10 native checks per run); all 29 local-CI tests and workflow drift checks passed.
- Native macOS acceptance: a real signed installation invoked its own Splash tool, queried OS camera permission through Rust, updated the live UI and returned a structured answer. Native button input, missing API fallback, capability/account/schema refusal, background callback suppression and closed-owner behavior passed. The reproducible driver and a dedicated macOS CI job are included; it does not claim model/peer-consent coverage.
- OAuth/backend suite: 92 passed, one optional OS-vault test ignored; includes real local HTTP fixtures and background-write refusal.
- Prompt-provenance regression: reproduced detached-timer escalation before the fix. Isolate suite 10/10, script core 61/61, script std 6 unit + 1 headless, unwind 2/2 passed. Full Makepad widget suite: 280 passed, 5 failed; the exact unchanged baseline has the same five failures (font fallback, grid overflow and widget-tree lookup). These are reported, not counted as passes.
- App Hub runner/VM and native bundled-font checks are covered by [App Hub #138](https://github.com/OctoSense-org/OctoSense-App-Hub/pull/138); font fallback by [renderer #79](https://github.com/OctoSense-org/OctoScript-Makepad/pull/79).

Limits: this is source integration, not a published host binary or OnePlus 6 acceptance. No live provider/model or physical permission approval is claimed. Windows/Linux embedded WebReader is handled separately in [PR #361](https://github.com/OctoSense-org/OctoSense/pull/361). Android Google login, new device adapters outside Android/macOS, script cold-start and Wasm remain unsupported.

title: Add native signed app-tool acceptance runner
body:
Add a configurable native acceptance host for signed app-owned Splash tools. It admits a stamped bundle with an ephemeral test signature, loads the live UI under its app policy, invokes the production app-tool binding, records exact results/refusals, and keeps the UI available to the Makepad instrument driver. Isolated data directories carry an app/digest marker for safe restart.

This PR is stacked on #402 for its callback/runtime fixes. It does not register model, account or Glance services. The caller enters after the production peer/consent relay, so this is not evidence of agent consent or a model-generated tool call.

Validation on the exact release binary (SHA-256 `e24b9934c1b4df762f63bf16ebab428fc91504e05a9948d74dc6f708bc8b18d6`):

- API Migration Lab: initial state, empty-input refusal, multiline Unicode edits, local save, unavailable model/Glance errors without draft loss, and exact persisted state after restart all passed.
- Tool State: signed admission, an actual `app_tool` action updating the live UI, a native manual edit, and a restarted read tool returning that persisted revision all passed. Malformed arguments, an incorrect account, an undeclared tool and an unregistered owner were refused.
- Actual negative controls failed as expected: replacing `app_tool` with the legacy `on_agent_tool` produced `app_handler_missing`; removing `script-tools-v1` was rejected at binding.
- All seven native Metal screenshots were visually inspected. Bilingual runner docs and a compact source/binary-bound receipt are included.

The tested runner source is `77b7c6b5`; the prepared runtime tree is `9121e900f18d5d6f22840ed330c1d7931231509a`. The follow-up commit records evidence without changing Rust source. Tests use synthetic data and isolated profiles, with no provider/private-account access. Public Store install, phone acceptance, model/provider effects and full-shell consent remain unverified. The Flow examples and their drivers are in [App Flow #176](https://github.com/OctoSense-org/OctoSense-App-Flow/pull/176); no catalog change is made here.

title: Add scoped connected-app services and reviewed agent tool mappings
body:
Ordinary App Hub apps need reusable provider services without receiving tokens or declaring first-party system IDs. Add explicit `auth`, `github`, `gcalendar` and `gmail` capabilities and signed, reviewed `host_method` mappings for app-owned tools. Admission keeps app namespace, target-family grants, private-data flags and minimum risk checks; approval/remote-write endpoints are excluded.

Keep host-sheet text, keyboard, IME, clipboard and pointer-release events out of the underlying app. A shared input classifier is used by the installed runner and OctoSense’s foreground Glance workspace; the runner captures its host surface references before app evaluation. Also retire host sheets before replacing them. A queued request or late reply from the prior sheet can no longer act on its replacement, including when a Splash heap address is reused.

Depends on #96 for the existing media-capability/system-pack changes. [OctoSense #347](https://github.com/OctoSense-org/OctoSense/pull/347) implements the services; [App Design Flow #154](https://github.com/OctoSense-org/OctoScript-App-Design-Flow/pull/154) carries the three connected sample apps. This PR alone does not configure OAuth or run an agent.

Validation: contract/policy suites passed, including 29 agent-bundle tests; all 20 appstore tests passed, including real Splash/pump replacement and native CardAppView modal-input regressions. GitHub contract and semver checks passed on `5c7a13f92fa25d36ba1fe7fb99dc9fb1b235f8d3`. Live provider and device acceptance are outside this repository and remain pending. No production catalog, publisher key or private account data changed.

title: Admission: accept or reject a submission on host API and widget support
body:
## Problem

Admission (`hub check`) cannot tell whether the host an app targets actually implements the APIs the app uses. Two kinds of dependency are invisible until runtime:

- **Widgets and script methods.** An app that uses a Makepad widget or widget method the host lacks fails only when the UI is realized (`ERR_UNKNOWN_TYPE`) or the method is called (`MethodNotFound`). Nothing in the manifest names them and admission does not inspect the source.
- **`host.request` targets.** An app can call a method its manifest never declares. The runtime refuses it, but admission passes it.

So a submission can be accepted that cannot run on the release it targets, and a reviewer finds out by hand.

## What exists today

- `host_api: { required: {"model.embeddings": 1}, optional: {…} }` plus `requires: ["host-api-v1"]`; `check_host_apis` → `check_available` compares them with the host's `available_versions()` and refuses install with a named reason (`this host does not implement required APIs: model.embeddings@1`).
- `KNOWN_CAPABILITIES` in app-contract lists every declarable capability, family-level and method-level.

The machinery is right; its coverage is not. Widgets and script methods are not in the registry, and nothing checks `host.request` targets or widget use at admission.

## Design

1. **Version the UI surface.** Enumerate the runtime's widgets and script methods as versioned features and publish them through `available_versions()`, so a host advertises exactly what it provides (e.g. `ui.video: 1`). Mark each host-API family as served for store apps, system apps only, or per platform.
2. **Let apps declare what they use** in the manifest, extending `host_api.required`.
3. **Check at both ends.** The host keeps running `check_available` at install; `hub check` runs the same comparison at submission, so a submission is accepted or refused with a named missing feature.
4. **Static scan as the author aid (prototyped).** Read the bundle's `.splash` sources, collect widget/type instantiations and `host.request` targets, subtract the app's own `let Name = Widget{…}` definitions and enum-variant values, and compare with the registry and `KNOWN_CAPABILITIES`. Report anything the target host does not define. This can run as a warning first and become a refusal once the registry (step 1) is authoritative.

## Prototype results

The step-4 scanner ran over the 36 current submissions whose submitted bundle ships Splash source, reading from fetched git objects (nothing executed) and scoped to the bundle whose manifest `id` matches the submission, since several repositories hold other apps beside it. Registry: the rc.1 pins (makepad `32d6415f`, Octoscript-Makepad `33dea2f1`, App Hub `ba36df05`).

- 0 use a widget type the rc.1 runtime does not define.
- 1 calls `host.request` targets the contract cannot grant (an app-private namespace), in a commit the author has since superseded.
- The gate already refuses an unknown capability that the manifest *declares* (`policy: app <id> requests unknown capability "photo.pick"`, seen on a sibling app in one repository). What it does not see today is a `host.request` to a target the manifest never names, or a widget the host lacks; the scan covers both.
- After subtracting app-defined components (`let Name = Widget{…}`) and enum-variant values, no false positives remained. Scoping mattered: a repo-wide pass had attributed a sibling app's native-extension widgets to the submission.

What the scan cannot decide is whether a declarable family actually serves a store app on the targeted release; that is what step 1's registry adds.

## Relation to the runtime-gate decision

With the per-app runtime gates being removed, the host API surface becomes the boundary. This registry then doubles as its specification: the same list says what an app may call and what a release implements.

## Open points

- Granularity: per widget, per method, or both, and how versions move.
- Where the check lives: `hub check` and the store install path share `check_available`; the scan is a `hub` subcommand or part of `check`.
- Reviewer output: name the missing feature and the first release that provides it.
